analysis.one_liner: Lets cable companies keep using all-in-one set-top boxes, repealing FCC rules meant to let competitors make devices.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee without a hearing or a vote, despite drawing 7 cosponsors — 4 Democrats and 3 Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the FCC from barring cable and satellite companies from using integrated set-top boxes — single devices that combine the security function and the viewing functions — and would repeal any existing rule doing so. That FCC requirement, adopted in 2007, was meant to let consumers buy competing devices from other companies instead of renting the cable company's box every month. Repealing it would hand the box back to the operators. The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in subcommittee when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: "Cable, satellite, and telephone-company video providers — the multichannel video programming distributors the bill names. Repealing the integration-ban authority lets them put security back inside their own boxes, ending the costs of supporting separable CableCARD security and preserving the leasing model in which nearly every subscriber rents the operator's box each month. It also removes the threat of a future FCC reopening the device market to independent competitors."

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the FCC from adopting any rule or policy barring a multichannel video programming distributor — a cable, satellite, or telephone-company video provider — from using navigation devices that combine conditional access (security) and other functions in one integrated set-top box.

Repeals any such existing FCC rule or policy on the day of enactment and orders the FCC to remove it from its rules — erasing the requirement that cable boxes use separable security, which was designed to let consumers attach their own devices.

With security built back into the operator's own box, third parties cannot practically make competing devices, so operators keep the leasing model in which subscribers pay a monthly rental fee per box instead of buying a device at retail.

analysis.who_pays: "Cable subscribers, most of whom rent a box from their provider each month and would keep facing a market where the operator's integrated box is the only real option — no retail device competition to pressure rental fees. Independent device makers such as TiVo would also lose the legal route the rule gave them into cable households."
analysis.who_pays_short: Cable subscribers paying monthly box rentals

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip the FCC of the authority to require separate security functions — the mechanism by which a subscriber could buy a competing device instead of renting the cable company's box month after month — leaving rental fees and operator control of the box untouched.

The new subsection says nothing in the law authorizes any FCC rule or policy prohibiting integrated devices, and orders any existing rule struck from the FCC's books, so a future FCC could not revive device competition even with better enforcement.

An honest supporter's case: the integration ban imposed real equipment costs on operators and never delivered a thriving retail device market. That objection has substance — but the bill's remedy was to repeal the requirement permanently rather than fix or replace it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: "Operators had a fair point that the separable-security mandate added costs and never produced the robust retail market Congress hoped for. But the bill's answer was to repeal it outright and permanently bar the FCC from re-imposing it, ending the only legal route to owning rather than renting the box. The costs — continued rental fees and operator control of the home's main video device — would land on subscribers; the savings would land on the providers. On balance the bill traded a consumer-competition safeguard for operator convenience, and happily for subscribers it never became law."

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then its communications subcommittee, never got a hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on September 26, 2013 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Referred to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology on September 27, 2013 — the day after introduction.
The full action record lists no further activity: no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever held.
The bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
It had attracted 7 cosponsors — 4 House Democrats and 3 House Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable subscribers: the repeal never advanced, so the FCC kept its legal authority under the existing statute to push for devices that compete with the cable company's rental box. Cable and satellite operators did not get the rule change they wanted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers; operators never got their repeal

for.name: Rep. Bob Latta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 26, 2013 to bar the FCC from prohibiting integrated set-top boxes.

for.name: Rep. Gene Green
for.what_they_did: Joined Latta in introducing the bill the day it was filed.

for.name: 7 cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors on the Energy and Commerce Committee's bill file
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support: 4 House Democrats and 3 House Republicans.

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in his committee after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and it died at the subcommittee stage.

against.name: Rep. Greg Walden
against.role: Chair, Subcommittee on Communications and Technology
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 27, 2013; the subcommittee never took the bill up.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — a Republican sponsor joined by a senior Texas Democrat as co-introducer, with cosponsors split 4 Democrats and 3 Republicans — and because the bill never reached a floor vote, no formal opposition was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Cable, satellite, and telephone-company video providers (multichannel video programming distributors)
industries.note: The bill would let operators put security back inside their own boxes, shedding the cost of supporting separable security and preserving the monthly box-rental fee nearly every subscriber pays. It would also permanently foreclose a future FCC effort to reopen the device market to competitors.

industries.industry: Independent set-top box and consumer-electronics makers (e.g., TiVo and retail device makers)
industries.note: The rule the bill repeals was the legal opening for non-cable devices to reach cable subscribers at retail. With security integrated into the operator's box, independent devices would again be shut out of most cable homes.
